title: API Design & Edge Security: Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision notes on choosing between REST, gRPC and GraphQL, designing resource URLs, pagination, versioning and idempotency, then fronting APIs with gateways and BFFs, auth (OAuth 2.0, JWT) and edge rate limits.

chapters.title: API Styles: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
points: REST: resources identified by URLs, manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET safe/idempotent, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial, DELETE), stateless, JSON over HTTP, cacheable via HTTP caching
gRPC: contract-first with Protobuf over HTTP/2; binary, strongly typed, supports unary, server-streaming, client-streaming and bidirectional streaming; best for internal service-to-service calls
GraphQL: single endpoint, client sends a query naming exactly the fields it needs; schema with queries, mutations, subscriptions; solves over-fetching and under-fetching

Comparison row: REST = simple, cacheable, public APIs; gRPC = fastest, streaming, needs HTTP/2 (poor browser support without grpc-web); GraphQL = flexible for many clients, harder to cache (POST to one URL) and the N+1 resolver problem needs DataLoader batching
Mistake: choosing GraphQL or gRPC by hype; default to REST for public APIs, gRPC internally, GraphQL when many clients need different shapes of the same data

chapters.title: REST Design: Naming, Pagination, Versioning, Idempotency
points: Resource naming: plural nouns, no verbs in the path, hierarchy for ownership: GET /users/42/orders, POST /orders (not /createOrder); use lowercase kebab-case; actions that don't fit CRUD become sub-resources, e.g. POST /orders/42/cancel
Offset pagination: ?limit=20&offset=40; simple and allows jumping to a page, but slow on deep offsets (DB scans and discards rows) and skips or duplicates rows when data changes mid-browse

Cursor pagination: ?limit=20&cursor=<opaque token> encoding the last seen sort key (WHERE id > last ORDER BY id); stable under inserts, fast with an index, but no random page jump; return next_cursor in the response

Versioning: URL path /v1/users (most common, explicit), header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) or query param; only bump the major version for breaking changes; adding optional fields is non-breaking; announce deprecation with a Sunset header

Idempotency keys: client sends Idempotency-Key: <uuid> on POST; server stores key with the first response and replays it on retries, so a network retry never double-charges; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, POST is not; keys expire after about 24h and a reused key with a different body returns 422

chapters.title: API Gateway and Backend-for-Frontend
points: API gateway: single entry point in front of microservices that handles routing, TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, request/response transformation, caching and logging
Gateway request flow: client → gateway (authenticate, rate limit, route) → service; the gateway centralises cross-cutting concerns so each service does not reimplement them
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): one tailored backend per client type (web, mobile, partner) that aggregates and reshapes downstream calls, so mobile gets a lean payload and web gets a rich one
Comparison: gateway = shared, one per system, cross-cutting policy; BFF = per-client, owned by the frontend team, aggregation and shaping logic
Mistake: putting business logic in the gateway, which turns it into a single point of failure and a team bottleneck; keep it thin, run it redundant and keep domain rules in the services

chapters.title: Authentication vs Authorization, OAuth 2.0 and JWT
points: Authentication (authn) = who are you (401 Unauthorized when missing or invalid credentials); authorization (authz) = what may you do (403 Forbidden when identity is known but access is denied)

OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization, not authentication: roles are resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server; the client gets a scoped access token instead of the user's password; OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top for authentication

Authorization Code flow with PKCE is the standard for web, SPA and mobile: redirect user to the authorization server, receive a code, exchange code plus code_verifier for tokens; Client Credentials flow is for machine-to-machine; the Implicit flow is deprecated

JWT = header.payload.signature, each base64url encoded; the payload carries claims (sub, iss, aud, exp, scope); the signature (HS256 shared secret or RS256/ES256 key pair) proves integrity, but the payload is NOT encrypted so never put secrets in it

Mistakes: accepting alg none or not pinning the algorithm, not validating exp, iss and aud, storing tokens in localStorage (XSS), long-lived access tokens with no revocation path; use short expiry (5-15 min) plus a rotating refresh token

chapters.title: Edge Rate Limiting
points: Rate limiting at the edge (CDN, WAF or gateway) rejects abusive traffic before it reaches your origin; return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header plus X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers
Token bucket: bucket holds N tokens refilled at a fixed rate, each request spends one; allows bursts up to N while holding the average rate; the most common choice
Fixed window counter is cheap but allows a double burst at window boundaries; sliding window (log or counter) smooths this at a higher memory cost; leaky bucket enforces a constant output rate

Choose the limit key deliberately: per API key or user for authenticated traffic, per IP for anonymous traffic (shared NATs punish many users); use a shared store like Redis so limits hold across gateway instances
Mistake: limiting only at the app layer so the origin still pays for the traffic, and clients that retry immediately on 429; clients should use exponential backoff with jitter

chapters.title: API Design Cheat Sheet
points: Style pick: REST for public and cacheable, gRPC for internal and streaming, GraphQL for many clients with varying data needs
URL rules: plural nouns, no verbs, nest for ownership; pagination: offset = simple but drifts, cursor = stable and fast; version in the path /v1 and bump only on breaking changes
Idempotency: Idempotency-Key header on POST, server replays the stored response; status codes: 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 429 rate limited, 422 key reuse with a different body
Auth: OAuth 2.0 = delegated authorization, OIDC = identity; use Auth Code + PKCE for users, Client Credentials for services; JWT = signed not encrypted, always validate alg, exp, iss and aud
Edge: gateway for cross-cutting policy, BFF per client type, token bucket rate limit keyed by API key, answer with 429 + Retry-After and have clients back off with jitter
